claim: NEDD8 is a ubiquitin-like modifier most well-studied for its role in activating the largest family of ubiquitin E3 ligases, the cullin-RING ligases (CRLs).
source: NEDD8 is a ubiquitin-like modifier most well-studied for its role in activating the largest family of ubiquitin E3 ligases, the cullin-RING ligases (CRLs).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about NEDD8's primary function.

claim: Overexpression of exogenous NEDD8 can trigger NEDD8 conjugation through the ubiquitylation machinery.
source: overexpression of exogenous NEDD8 can trigger NEDD8 conjugation through the ubiquitylation machinery
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hjerpe et al., 2012 in the Introduction section.

claim: A deconjugation-resistant form of NEDD8 (L73P mutant) was developed to stabilize the neddylated form of cullins and other non-cullin substrates.
source: Here, we developed a deconjugation-resistant form of NEDD8 to stabilize the neddylated form of cullins and other non-cullin substrates.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Ubc12, a NEDD8-specific E2 conjugating enzyme, is a substrate for auto-neddylation.
source: we identified Ubc12, a NEDD8-specific E2 conjugating enzyme, as a substrate for auto-neddylation
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by MS data in Figure 1F and validation experiments in Figure 2.

claim: SENP8/DEN1 is the protease that counteracts Ubc12 auto-neddylation.
source: we characterized SENP8/DEN1 as the protease that counteracts Ubc12 auto-neddylation
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro deneddylation assays in Figure 3 and cellular experiments.

claim: SENP8-deficient cells show aberrant neddylation of Ubc12 and other NEDD8 conjugation pathway components.
source: observed aberrant neddylation of Ubc12 and other NEDD8 conjugation pathway components in SENP8-deficient cells
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and MS data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Loss of SENP8 function contributes to accumulation of CRL substrates.
source: loss of SENP8 function contributes to accumulation of CRL substrates
evidence: This is demonstrated through SILAC-MS analysis and immunoblotting in Figure 7.

claim: Loss of SENP8 function contributes to defective cell cycle progression.
source: loss of SENP8 function contributes to accumulation of CRL substrates and defective cell cycle progression
evidence: This is shown through flow cytometry analysis in Figure 6.

claim: Neddylation is catalyzed through an enzymatic cascade consisting of an E1-activating enzyme complex (NAE1/APPBP1-UBA3), two E2 enzymes (Ubc12/Ube2M and Ube2F) and several E3 enzymes such as Rbx1 and Rbx2.
source: Like ubiquitylation, neddylation is catalyzed through an enzymatic cascade consisting of an E1-activating enzyme complex (NAE1/APPBP1-UBA3), two E2 enzymes (Ubc12/Ube2M and Ube2F) and several E3 enzymes such as Really Interesting New Gene (RING)-box protein 1 (Rbx1) and its close homologue Rbx2 (reviewed in [Soucy et al., 2010; Enchev et al., 2014; Brown and Jackson, 2015]).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple review citations.

claim: NEDD8 transfer from the E2 to a lysine residue within the cullin promotes conformational changes that increase the catalytic activity of the CRL.
source: NEDD8 transfer from the E2 to a lysine (Lys) residue within the cullin promotes conformational changes that increase the catalytic activity of the CRL, while also blocking the binding of the CRL exchange factor CAND1 (Duda et al., 2008; Saha and Deshaies, 2008; Pierce et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: NEDD8 conjugation to cullin subunits controls approximately 10-20% of ubiquitylation events in cells.
source: NEDD8 ligation to cullins controls a high proportion of ubiquitylation events in cells (~10–20%) (Soucy et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soucy et al., 2009.

claim: MLN4924 is an inhibitor of the NEDD8 E1 enzyme that potently and rapidly suppresses neddylation in cells.
source: An inhibitor of the NEDD8 E1 enzyme, MLN4924, has been recently developed and shown to potently and rapidly suppress neddylation in cells, thereby inhibiting CRL activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soucy et al., 2009, 2010 and Brownell et al., 2010.

claim: MLN4924 has demonstrated antitumor activity in several human tumor xenografts and hematological malignancies in preclinical studies.
source: Significantly, preclinical studies using MLN4924 have demonstrated its antitumor activity in several human tumor xenografts and hematological malignancies (Soucy et al., 2009, 2010; Brownell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to preclinical studies.

claim: p53 is a non-cullin neddylation target.
source: Among this list of proteins are p53 (Xirodimas et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xirodimas et al., 2004.

claim: E2F1 is a non-cullin neddylation target.
source: E2F1 (Loftus et al., 2012; Aoki et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Loftus et al., 2012 and Aoki et al., 2013.

claim: Ribosomal protein L11 is a non-cullin neddylation target.
source: ribosomal protein L11 (Sundqvist et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sundqvist et al., 2009.

claim: Smurf1 is a non-cullin neddylation target.
source: Smurf1 (Xie et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xie et al., 2014.

claim: Histone H4 is a non-cullin neddylation target.
source: Histone H4 (Ma et al., 2013b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2013b.

claim: CSN5 is the major cullin deneddylase in human cells.
source: COP9 signalosome complex subunit 5 (CSN5), a metallo-protease and component of the eight-subunit COP9 signalosome complex (CSN), is the major cullin deneddylase in human cells (Lyapina et al., 2001; Cope, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lyapina et al., 2001 and Cope, 2002.

claim: CSN is specific for neddylated cullins.
source: CSN is specific for neddylated cullins (Lingaraju et al., 2014; Cavadini et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lingaraju et al., 2014 and Cavadini et al., 2016.

claim: SENP8 functions distinctly from CSN in deneddylating primarily non-cullin substrates.
source: Recently, a cysteine protease called SENP8 (also known as DEN1 or NEDP1) has been characterized that functions distinctly from CSN in deneddylating primarily non-cullin substrates (Chan et al., 2008; Mergner et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2008 and Mergner et al., 2015.

claim: SENP8 deneddylates hyper-neddylated cullins.
source: a cysteine protease called SENP8 (also known as DEN1 or NEDP1) has been characterized that functions distinctly from CSN in deneddylating primarily non-cullin substrates (Chan et al., 2008; Mergner et al., 2015) as well as hyper-neddylated cullins (Mendoza et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mendoza et al., 2003 and Wu et al., 2003.

claim: SENP8 selectively interacts with NEDD8 and not ubiquitin.
source: SENP8 selectively interacts with NEDD8 and not ubiquitin (Gan-Erdene et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gan-Erdene et al., 2003 and Shen et al., 2005.

claim: SENP8 plays a redundant role in proteolytic processing of the precursor form of NEDD8 in conjunction with UCHL3.
source: also plays a redundant role in proteolytic processing of the precursor form of NEDD8 in conjunction with ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase isozyme 3 (UCHL3) (Wada et al., 1998; Wu et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wada et al., 1998 and Wu et al., 2003.

claim: DEN1null and CSN5null Drosophila larvae show distinct neddylation defects, suggesting that the two enzymes have non-overlapping functions.
source: a previous study showed distinct neddylation defects in DEN1null versus CSN5null Drosophila larvae, suggesting that the two enzymes have non-overlapping functions (Chan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan et al., 2008.

claim: The L73P mutation in NEDD8 is located at the P4 position of the C-terminal cleavage site.
source: mutation of leucine (Leu) 73 in ubiquitin, located at the P4 position of the DUB cleavage site at the C-terminus, to proline (Pro)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B which displays the location of the L73P mutation.

claim: The L73P mutation in ubiquitin renders conjugated ubiquitin resistant to cleavage by a wide range of deubiquitinating enzymes.
source: We have previously demonstrated that mutation of leucine (Leu) 73 in ubiquitin, located at the P4 position of the DUB cleavage site at the C-terminus, to proline (Pro) renders conjugated ubiquitin resistant to cleavage by a wide range of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) (Békés et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Békés et al., 2013.

claim: The P4 position in NEDD8 is a leucine residue, analogous to ubiquitin.
source: The C-termini of Nedd8 and Ub are conserved, where the P4 position in NEDD8 is also a Leu residue.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and structural knowledge.

claim: NEDD8 L73P is resistant to CSN-mediated deconjugation from CUL1 in vitro.
source: While WT NEDD8 was readily deconjugated from CUL1 with increasing concentrations of CSN in the reaction, the L73P NEDD8 mutant was resistant to cleavage from CUL1 at all CSN concentrations.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1C showing in vitro deneddylation assays.

claim: Ortho-phenanthroline (OPT) completely inhibits the metalloprotease activity of CSN.
source: As expected, the addition of the zinc-chelator ortho-phenanthroline (OPT) to the reaction mixture completely inhibited the metalloprotease activity of CSN, and neither WT nor L73P NEDD8 were cleaved from CUL1 under these conditions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1C.

claim: FLAG-NEDD8-L73P shows increased recovery of modified CUL1 compared to FLAG-NEDD8-WT.
source: We observed increased recovery of FLAG-NEDD8-L73P-modified CUL1 compared to FLAG-NEDD8-WT-conjugated CUL1, likely reflecting the inability of the L73P mutant to be deneddylated in cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D immunoblot analysis.

claim: MLN4924 treatment blocks the conjugation of both endogenous NEDD8 and FLAG-NEDD8 to cullin substrates.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Soucy et al., 2009; Brownell et al., 2010), MLN4924 treatment blocked the conjugation of both endogenous NEDD8 and FLAG-NEDD8 to cullin substrates entirely (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1E and supported by citations.

claim: FLAG-NEDD8-WT and FLAG-NEDD8-L73P are incorporated into CUL1- and CUL2-conjugates at similar levels as endogenous NEDD8.
source: Importantly, immunoblot analyses showed that both FLAG-NEDD8-WT and FLAG-NEDD8-L73P were incorporated into CUL1- and CUL2- conjugates at similar levels as endogenous NEDD8 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E immunoblot analysis.

claim: FLAG-NEDD8-L73P immunoprecipitates show higher relative abundance of cullin substrates (CUL1, -2, -4A, and -4B) compared to FLAG-NEDD8-WT based on spectral counting.
source: As anticipated, both FLAG-NEDD8-WT and FLAG-NEDD8-L73P immunoprecipitated CUL1, −2, −4A, and −4B, although the relative abundance, based on spectral counting, of these cullin substrates was much higher in the FLAG-NEDD8-L73P IP samples (Figure 1F and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F spectral count data.

claim: The site of NEDD8 conjugation to Ubc12 is Lys3.
source: Upon further analysis of our MS results from the FLAG-NEDD8-L73P IP dataset, we determined that the site of NEDD8 conjugation to Ubc12 is Lys3, as we observed a K-ε-GG remnant, characteristic of trypic digestion of either NEDD8 or ubiquitin, at this site (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MS/MS spectrum in Figure 2A.

claim: The Ubc12 peptide containing Lys3 is acetylated at the N-terminus.
source: This Ubc12 peptide was also acetylated at the N-terminus, in agreement with previous observations (Scott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is observed in MS data and supported by citation to Scott et al., 2011.

claim: The Lys3 residue of Ubc12 is highly conserved across several eukaryotic orthologs.
source: Sequence alignments show that the Lys3 residue of Ubc12 is highly conserved across several eukaryotic orthologs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 2A.

claim: Ubc12 is modified by FLAG-NEDD8-L73P in a manner that is blocked by MLN4924 pretreatment.
source: Immunoblot analysis of identically prepared FLAG-NEDD8 IPs showed that Ubc12 is modified upon Dox-induced expression by FLAG-NEDD8-L73P, but not when pre-treated with MLN4924, (Figure 2B). suggesting that these represent neddylated Ubc12 species (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B immunoblot analysis.

claim: WT and L73P HA-tagged NEDD8 constructs, but not HA-tagged Ub constructs, form conjugates with co-transfected MycFlag-Ubc12 WT.
source: Both WT and L73P HA-tagged NEDD8 constructs, but not the analogous WT and L73P HA-tagged Ub constructs, formed conjugates with co-transfected MycFlag-Ubc12 WT in these experiments (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C co-IP experiments.

claim: Mutations in the NK0-Ubc12 mutant (all N-terminal Lys residues converted to Arg) block modification by co-transfected NEDD8-L73P.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, mutations introduced into the NK0-Ubc12 mutant sufficiently blocked modification by co-transfected NEDD8-L73P.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2D immunoblot analysis.

claim: Restoring a single Lys at position 3 (K3) in the NK0-Ubc12 mutant (N-K3) partially rescues the ability of Ubc12 to form conjugates with NEDD8-L73P.
source: Furthermore, restoring a single Lys at position 3 (K3) in the NK0-Ubc12 mutant (N-K3) partially rescued the ability of Ubc12 to form conjugates with NEDD8-L73P (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2D immunoblot analysis.

claim: N-terminal Lys sites, including K3, are critical for NEDD8 modification of Ubc12.
source: Altogether, these results provide strong evidence that Ubc12 is a bona fide substrate for neddylation, and that N-terminal Lys sites, including K3, are critical for NEDD8 modification of Ubc12.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis experiments in Figure 2D.

claim: The acetylated N-terminal Met in Ubc12 interacts with a hydrophobic pocket in DCN1 to promote cullin neddylation.
source: It was previously shown that the acetylated N-terminal Met in Ubc12 interacts with a hydrophobic pocket in the co-E3, DCN1 (DCUN1D1 in human cells), to promote cullin neddylation (Scott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scott et al., 2011.

claim: Only WT Ubc12, but not the NK0 mutant, can support modification with HA-NEDD8-L73P.
source: Consistent with our previous experiments, only the WT Ubc12 construct, but not the NK0 mutant, could support modification with HA-NEDD8-L73P, which likely contributed to reduced interaction to DCN1 and Cul3 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2E co-IP experiments.

claim: WT Ubc12 co-purifies with more DCN1 when it is not neddylated by HA-NEDD8-L73P co-expression.
source: Consistently, WT Ubc12 co-purified with more DCN1 when it was not neddylated by HA-NEDD8-L73P co-expression (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2F co-IP experiments.

claim: N-terminal neddylation of Ubc12 likely weakens binding to DCN1.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that N-terminal neddylation of Ubc12 likely weakens binding to DCN1, which in turn may influence downstream NEDD8 pathway function.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP experiments in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Treatment of cells with siRNAs targeting SENP8, but not CSN5, results in increased levels of Ubc12 conjugates.
source: Treatment of cells with siRNAs targeting SENP8, but not CSN5, resulted in increased levels of Ubc12 conjugates (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A immunoblot analysis.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of endogenous SENP8 results in increased levels of Ubc12 conjugates.
source: These results were corroborated by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of endogenous SENP8 using multiple sgRNA sequences in different cell lines (Figures 3B and 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3B and 5B immunoblot analyses.

claim: A band corresponding to di-neddylated Ubc12 is detected in SENP8 knockout cell lines but not parental cells.
source: In immunoblot analyses of IP samples, probing with antibodies against Ubc12 and NEDD8 detected a band of similar molecular weight corresponding to di-neddylated Ubc12 in both SENP8 knockout cell lines, but not the parental cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Higher molecular weight Ubc12 NEDD8-conjugates are no longer observed in SENP8-deficient cells following treatment with MLN4924.
source: Additionally, higher molecular weight Ubc12 NEDD8-conjugates were no longer observed in either siRNA-depleted (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or CRISPR-generated SENP8-deficient cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) following treatment with MLN4924.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Ubc12 undergoes auto-neddylation when incubated with the E1 enzyme, ATP, and recombinant NEDD8 (WT or L73P) in vitro.
source: As demonstrated previously (Huang et al., 2005), we observed that Ubc12 undergoes auto-neddylation when incubated with the E1 enzyme, ATP, and recombinant NEDD8 (WT or L73P) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3C in vitro assay and supported by citation.

claim: Ubc12 auto-neddylation occurs in cis via its own catalytic Cys residue.
source: We also showed that Ubc12 auto-neddylation occurs in cis via its own catalytic Cys residue, as the catalytically inactive mutant of Ubc12 (C111A) is not neddylated in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), even in the presence of additional WT Ubc12 or when transfected in cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: Recombinant SENP8 removes NEDD8 from auto-neddylated Ubc12 in reactions containing WT NEDD8, but not the L73P mutant.
source: This modification was removed when recombinant SENP8 was added to reactions containing WT NEDD8, but not the L73P mutant (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3C in vitro deneddylation assay.

claim: NEDD8 deconjugation from auto-neddylated Ubc12 occurs in the presence of SENP8, but not CSN.
source: Moreover, in titration experiments using different concentrations of recombinant SENP8 or CSN proteases, we further showed that NEDD8 deconjugation from auto-neddylated Ubc12 only occurs in the presence of SENP8, but not CSN (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3D in vitro deneddylation assay.

claim: SENP8 is the primary protease that regulates Ubc12 auto-neddylation both in vitro and in cells.
source: Taken together, these findings establish SENP8 as the primary protease that regulates Ubc12 auto-neddylation both in vitro and in cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined in vitro and cellular experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Immunoblotting analysis with an anti-NEDD8 antibody reveals a dramatic increase in protein neddylation in SENP8 knockout cells compared to control cells.
source: Supporting this notion, immunoblotting analysis of whole-cell extracts with an anti-NEDD8 antibody revealed a dramatic increase in protein neddylation in SENP8 knockout cells in comparison to control cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A immunoblot analysis.

claim: SENP8 is likely to restrict aberrant or hyper-neddylation of non-cullin substrates in normal steady-state conditions.
source: This suggests that SENP8 is likely to restrict aberrant or hyper-neddylation of non-cullin substrates in normal steady-state conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased neddylation observed in SENP8 knockout cells.

claim: K-ε-GG modification of Ubc12, Ube1C, DCUN1D5, and NEDD8 itself (K11 and K48) show large increases in relative abundance in SENP8 knockout cells.
source: Interestingly, many of these K-ε-GG modification changes were observed for proteins involved in the NEDD8 conjugation pathway, including not only Ubc12, but also Ube1C, DCUN1D5, and NEDD8 itself (K11 and K48).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and D quantitative MS data.

claim: A significant decrease in the NEDD8 modification of CUL5 is observed in SENP8-deficient cells.
source: We also observed a significant decrease in the NEDD8 modification of CUL5in the SENP8-deficient cell line (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and D quantitative MS data.

claim: SENP8 prevents aberrant or hyper-neddylation on a global level of multiple proteins within the NEDD8 conjugation network.
source: Overall, these results provide further evidence to suggest that SENP8 prevents aberrant or hyper-neddylation on a global level of multiple proteins within the NEDD8 conjugation network.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative MS results in Figure 4.

claim: Increased levels of NEDD8 conjugates, including di-neddylated species, of NAE1 (APPBP1)-UBA3, Ubc12, DCUN1D1 and DCUN1D5 are observed in SENP8-deficient cell lines.
source: We observed evidence for increased levels of NEDD8 conjugates, and in several cases even di-neddylated (N82) species, of several NEDD8 pathway constituents in all SENP8-deficient cell lines tested, including NAE1 (APPBP1)-UBA3, Ubc12, and DCUN1D1 and DCUN1D5 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B immunoblot analysis.

claim: Relative binding of endogenous Ubc12 to DCN1 is reduced in the SENP8-deficient background compared to SENP8-corrected cells.
source: In agreement with our analyses in Figure 2, we also showed that relative binding of endogenous Ubc12 to DCN1 was reduced in the SENP8-deficient background in comparison to SENP8-corrected cells, suggesting that the aberrant neddylation observed in SENP8 knockout cells may contribute to a weakened Ubc12-DCN1 interaction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A co-IP experiments.

claim: A decrease in total levels of the E2 conjugating enzyme UBE2F is observed in SENP8 knockout cell lines.
source: Intriguingly, we also observed a decrease in total levels of the E2 conjugating enzyme UBE2F in the SENP8 knockout cell lines (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B immunoblot analysis.

claim: UBE2F has a unique preference for CUL5 neddylation.
source: A previous study demonstrated that while Ubc12 targets all other cullin subunits for activation, UBE2F has a unique preference for CUL5 neddylation (Huang et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2009a.

claim: A marked decrease in CUL5 and CUL1 neddylation is observed in SENP8-deficient cells.
source: Consistently, we observed a marked decrease in CUL5 as well as CUL1 neddylation in SENP8-deficient cells, whereas the neddylation of other cullin subunits was not substantially impacted (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5C immunoblot analysis.

claim: The neddylation defects observed in SENP8 knockout cells are reversed by complementation with ectopically expressed WT SENP8.
source: Importantly, the neddylation defects observed in SENP8 knockout cells were reversed by complementation with ectopically expressed WT SENP8 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5D immunoblot analysis.

claim: Overexpression of WT Ubc12 and DCN1 constructs in SENP8-deficient cells restores CUL1 and CUL5 neddylation levels.
source: We also observed a restoration of CUL1 and CUL5 neddylation levels when we overexpressed WT Ubc12 and DCN1 constructs in SENP8-deficient cells, further suggesting that loss of SENP8 affects optimal Ubc12/DCN1 function (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SENP8-deficient cells show accelerated cell growth compared to parental HeLa cells.
source: Notably, we observed that the SENP8-deficient cells showed accelerated cell growth in comparison to parental HeLa cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B cell growth assay.

claim: Loss of SENP8 contributes to a reduction in the subpopulation of G1 cells and a concomitant increase of cells in S and G2/M phases.
source: Strikingly, we found that loss of SENP8 contributes to notable changes in the cell cycle profiles of asynchronously dividing cells, including a reduction in the subpopulation of G1 cells, and a concomitant increase of cells in S and G2/M phases (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C and D flow cytometry analysis.

claim: The reduction in G1 phase cells observed in SENP8-deficient cells is partially rescued through complementation with WT SENP8.
source: Importantly, the reduction in G1 phase cells observed in SENP8-deficient cells was partially rescued through complementation with WT SENP8 (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C and D flow cytometry analysis.

claim: EdU incorporation begins at 6-8 hr following release from nocodozole in parental HeLa cells.
source: Interestingly, while EdU incorporation normally begins at 6–8 hr following release from nocodozole in the parental HeLa cell line, the accumulation of EdU positive cells occurs earlier at 4–6 hr in SENP8 knockout cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6E flow cytometry analysis.

claim: The accumulation of EdU positive cells occurs earlier at 4-6 hr in SENP8 knockout cells following release from nocodozole.
source: Interestingly, while EdU incorporation normally begins at 6–8 hr following release from nocodozole in the parental HeLa cell line, the accumulation of EdU positive cells occurs earlier at 4–6 hr in SENP8 knockout cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6E flow cytometry analysis.

claim: Premature EdU incorporation in SENP8 knockout cells can be partially reversed by complementation with wild-type SENP8.
source: This premature EdU incorporation could be partially reversed by complementation with wild-type SENP8 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6E flow cytometry analysis.

claim: SENP8 function is important in maintaining proper cell growth and G1/S cell cycle progression.
source: Collectively, these results show that SENP8 function is important in maintaining proper cell growth and G1/S cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is concluded from the cell cycle and growth experiments in Figure 6.

claim: K-ε-GG-modified peptides from proteins involved in cell proliferation are relatively more abundant in WT cells versus SENP8 knockout cells treated with MG132.
source: Interestingly, K-ε-GG-modified peptides from proteins involved in cell proliferation were relatively more abundant in WT cells versus SENP8 knockout cells (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), indicative of enhanced ubiquitylation of these targets.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7C SILAC-MS analysis.

claim: Notable targets with reduced ubiquitylation status in SENP8 knockout cells include Cdc25A, UHRF1, and β-catenin.
source: Notable targets with reduced ubiquitylation status in SENP8 knockout cells include substrates of the Cul1-based Skp1/Cul1/F-box protein (SCF)βTRCP E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, such as Cdc25A (Donzelli et al., 2002; Busino et al., 2003; Jin et al., 2003), UHRF1 (ICBP90) (Chen et al., 2013), and β-catenin (Latres et al., 1999; Walker et al., 2015)
evidence: This is identified from SILAC-MS data and supported by citations.

claim: SENP8 deficiency results in the prolonged half-life of Cdc25A in cycloheximide chase assays.
source: SENP8 deficiency results in the prolonged half-life of Cdc25A in cycloheximide chase assays, a protein which normally exhibits very rapid turnover in human cells (Busino et al., 2003) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7D cycloheximide chase assay and supported by citation.

claim: SENP8 loss contributes to reduced accumulation of higher molecular weight species of Cdc25A following MG132 treatment, indicative of decreased Cdc25A polyubiquitylation.
source: SENP8 loss also contributes to the reduced accumulation of higher molecular weight species of Cdc25A following MG132 treatment, indicative of decreased Cdc25A polyubiquitylation in comparison to WT cells. (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Asynchronous SENP8-deficient cells show increased total levels of Cdt1, Set8, and p21.
source: Furthermore, asynchronous SENP8-deficient cells show increased total levels of proteins identified by our MS screen, as well as other key substrates of the SCFSkp2, CRL4Cdt2, and SCFFbw7 E3 ubiquitin ligases with involvement in DNA replication and cell cycle control. These proteins include the origin licensing factor Cdt1 (Li et al., 2003; Jin et al., 2006; Nishitani et al., 2006), the histone H4 lysine 20 monomethylase Set8 (PR-Set7) (Abbas et al., 2010; Centore et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2010), the cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitor p21 (Bornstein et al., 2003; Abbas et al., 2008) (Figure 7E)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7E immunoblot analysis and supported by citations.

claim: Asynchronous SENP8-deficient cells show increased total levels of Cyclin E1.
source: the regulatory cyclin for CDK2, Cyclin E1 (Koepp et al., 2001; Hao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7E immunoblot analysis and supported by citations.

claim: The characteristic G1/S degradation patterns of both Cdc25A and UHRF1 are substantially altered in SENP8-deficient cells.
source: Notably, the characteristic G1/S degradation patterns of both Cdc25A and UHRF1, identified from our SILAC-MS screen in Figure 7B, were substantially altered in SENP8-deficient cells (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7F immunoblot analysis of synchronized cells.

claim: SENP8-deficient cells show increased levels of the E2F targets Cyclin E1 and Cyclin A2.
source: Accompanying the increased stability of these substrates, we found other evidence to support premature S phase entry in SENP8-deficient cells, such as increased levels of the E2F targets Cyclin E1 and Cyclin A2
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7F immunoblot analysis and supported by citations.

claim: SENP8-deficient cells show decreased accumulation of the G1 cyclin Cyclin D1 and the CDK inhibitor p27.
source: and decreased accumulation of the G1 cyclin Cyclin D1 and the CDK inhibitor p27 (Resnitzky et al., 1994; Soucek et al., 1997; Sigl et al., 2009; Yuan et al., 2014) (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7F immunoblot analysis and supported by citations.

claim: The increased stabilization of CRL substrates such as Cdc25A, UHRF1, and other factors likely underlies the accelerated S phase entry and loss of proper G1/S phase regulation in SENP8-deficient cells.
source: Thus, we speculate that the increased stabilization of CRL substrates such as Cdc25A, UHRF1, and probably several other factors underlie the accelerated S phase entry and loss of proper G1/S phase regulation in SENP8-deficient cells.
evidence: This is speculated based on the combined data from Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Cdc25A acts as a major regulator of both the G1/S and G2/M cell cycle transitions by dephosphorylating and activating Cyclin E/Cdk2 and Cyclin B/Cdk1 complexes.
source: Cdc25A acts as a major regulator of both the G1/S and G2/M cell cycle transitions by dephosphorylating and activating Cyclin E/Cdk2 and Cyclin B/Cdk1 complexes, respectively (Strausfeld et al., 1991; Blomberg and Hoffmann, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Overexpression of Cdc25A results in shortening of G1 phase and increased cyclin E- and cyclin A-associated kinase activity.
source: Several reports have observed shortening of G1 phase and increased cyclin E- and cyclin A-associated kinase activity following overexpression of Cdc25A (Blomberg and Hoffmann, 1999; Sexl et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The decreased CRL function accompanying SENP8 loss does not affect all CRL substrates uniformly and is likely to have substrate-specific effects.
source: It is also apparent from our studies that the decreased CRL function accompanying SENP8 loss does not affect all CRL substrates uniformly and is likely to have substrate-specific effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that not all CRL substrates are equally affected.

claim: SENP8 depletion does not result in a significant increase in cells with >4C DNA content or induction of a DNA damage response.
source: For example, SENP8 depletion does not entirely phenocopy the effects of complete inhibition of CRL activity following MLN4924 treatment, as we did not see a significant increase in cells with >4C DNA content (indicative of cells undergoing multiple rounds of replication without cell division, or re-replication) or induction of a DNA damage response in SENP8 knockout cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments.

claim: CSN inhibition results in substrate-specific stabilization dependent on auto-ubiquitylation of unique substrate recognition modules of CRLs.
source: Similarly, using a CSN5-specific inhibitor developed by Novartis, it was recently shown that CSN inhibition does not have pleiotropic effects on all CRL substrates as MLN4924 treatment does (Schlierf et al., 2016), but results in substrate-specific stabilization. This effect was shown to be dependent on the auto-ubiquitylation of unique substrate recognition modules of CRLs following sustained neddylation and activation of CRL complexes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlierf et al., 2016.

claim: There is a correlation between overactivation of NEDD8 pathway components (including NEDD8, UBA3, NAE1, and Ubc12) and cancer progression and poor prognosis in human lung cancers.
source: Several recent studies have observed a correlation between overactivation of NEDD8 pathway components, including NEDD8, UBA3, NAE1, and Ubc12, with cancer progression and poor prognosis in human lung cancers (Li et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: There is a correlation between overactivation of NEDD8 pathway components and cancer progression and poor prognosis in colorectal cancers.
source: colorectal cancers (Xie et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xie et al., 2014.

claim: There is a correlation between overactivation of NEDD8 pathway components and cancer progression and poor prognosis in glioblastomas.
source: and glioblastomas (Hua et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hua et al., 2015.

claim: Auto-neddylation within the NEDD8 pathway may represent a quality control mechanism to limit adverse consequences associated with elevated NEDD8 conjugation and CRL activity.
source: Thus, auto-neddylation within the NEDD8 pathway may represent a deliberate quality control mechanism to limit adverse consequences associated with elevated NEDD8 conjugation and CRL activity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of the study.

claim: NEDD8 conjugation to Ubc12 and other components occurs at defined Lys residues which are evolutionarily conserved across species.
source: Consistent with this notion, we observed in our own study that NEDD8 conjugation to Ubc12 and other components occurs at defined Lys residues, which are evolutionarily conserved across species.
evidence: This is observed from the MS data and sequence alignments in the study.

claim: SENP8 is a key regulator of the NEDD8 pathway.
source: Nevertheless, our study characterizes the SENP8 protease as a key regulator of the NEDD8 pathway
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive characterization in the study.

claim: SENP8 is a potential pharmacological target to control CRL-mediated processes in cells.
source: implicating SENP8 as a potential pharmacological target to control CRL-mediated processes in cells.
evidence: This is speculated based on the functional importance of SENP8 demonstrated in the study.
